Key Characteristics & Etiology: Systemic autoimmune disease with strong female predominance (9:1); peak onset 15-45 yrs; strongly associated with HLA-DR2 and HLA-DR3.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Type III (immune complex) and Type II hypersensitivity; loss of self-tolerance leads to antinuclear autoantibody production, immune complex deposition in tissues, complement activation, and organ damage.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Malar 'butterfly' rash (spares nasolabial folds), discoid rash, photosensitivity, oral/nasal painless ulcers, non-erosive arthritis, serositis (pleuritis, pericarditis), renal involvement (lupus nephritis), CNS lupus (seizures, psychosis).
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: ANA (sensitive >95% screening test); Anti-dsDNA (highly specific, correlates with disease activity & nephritis); Anti-Smith (most specific); decreased C3/C4 complement levels; Hydroxychloroquine (mainstay for all), Steroids, Cyclophosphamide/Belimumab for nephritis.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Chronic systemic inflammatory autoimmune disease primarily targetting synovial joints; female-to-male ratio 3:1; linked to HLA-DR4.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Autoimmune synovitis with pannus formation (proliferative synovial membrane) that erodes articular cartilage and underlying bone; driven by TNF-alpha, IL-1, and IL-6.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Symmetrical polyarthritis affecting PIP, MCP, and MTP joints (spares DIP joints); morning stiffness >1 hour; joint deformities (ulnar deviation, Swan-neck, Boutonniere); extra-articular features (rheumatoid nodules, interstitial lung disease, pericarditis, Felty syndrome).
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Anti-Citrullinated Protein Antibodies (Anti-CCP / ACPA, 98% specific); Rheumatoid Factor (RF); elevated ESR/CRP; X-ray showing juxta-articular osteopenia and joint space narrowing; Early DMARD therapy (Methotrexate + Folic acid mainstay, Leflunomide, Biologics like Anti-TNF Etanercept/Infliximab).

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Prototypic seronegative spondyloarthropathy; strong association with HLA-B27 (>90%); predominantly affects young males (15-30 yrs).
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Chronic inflammation at entheses (sites of tendon/ligament attachment to bone), particularly sacroiliac joints, followed by progressive ossification, syndesmophyte formation, and spinal fusion.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Inflammatory back pain (insidious onset <45 yrs, improves with exercise, worsens with rest, nocturnal awakenings), morning stiffness, reduced spinal mobility (Schober's test <5 cm expansion), acute anterior uveitis (painful red eye), apical lung fibrosis, aortic regurgitation.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Negative RF/Anti-CCP; positive HLA-B27; X-ray/MRI showing sacroiliitis, 'bamboo spine' (bridging syndesmophytes), dagger sign; First-line: NSAIDs (continuous), exercise/physiotherapy; Secukinumab (IL-17i) or Anti-TNF agents for refractory cases.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Metabolic disease characterized by hyperuricemia (serum urate > 6.8 mg/dL / >400 umol/L); more common in men; triggered by purine-rich diet, alcohol, loop diuretics, or renal impairment.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Supersaturation and deposition of monosodium urate (MSU) crystals in synovial fluid and soft tissues, triggering inflammasome activation, IL-1beta release, and severe neutrophilic joint inflammation.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Monoarthritis presenting as sudden onset of excruciating pain, swelling, erythema, and warmth at 1st metatarsophalangeal joint (Podagra); tophi formation (chalky urate deposits in ears, tendons, joints) in chronic gout; renal calculi.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Arthrocentesis: Needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals under polarized light; Acute attack: Colchicine, NSAIDs (Indomethacin/Naproxen), or Intra-articular/Oral Steroids; Chronic urate-lowering therapy: Allopurinol (xanthine oxidase inhibitor) or Febuxostat (start AFTER acute attack subsides).

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Deposition of calcium pyrophosphate crystals in hyaline and fibrocartilage; common in elderly; associated with hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis, hypomagnesemia, and hypothyroidism.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Precipitation of CPPD crystals in articular cartilage leads to shedding into joint space, provoking inflammatory response resembling acute gout or osteoarthritis.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Acute monoarthritis or oligoarthritis, most commonly affecting large joints like the knee, wrist, or shoulder; joint effusion and tenderness; chronic CPPD arthropathy resembles OA.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Arthrocentesis: Rhomboid-shaped, weakly positively birefringent crystals; X-ray shows chondrocalcinosis (linear calcification of articular cartilage/fibrocartilage menisci); Management: Intra-articular steroid injection, oral NSAIDs, or Colchicine.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Autoimmune disorder characterized by vascular dysfunction, autoimmunity, and widespread tissue fibrosis affecting skin and internal organs; marked female excess.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Endothelial injury causes microvascular obliteration; dysregulated fibroblast activation leads to excessive deposition of collagen and extracellular matrix in skin, lungs, GI tract, and kidneys.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Limited Cutaneous (CREST syndrome: Calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia); Diffuse Cutaneous (rapid skin thickening proximal to elbows/knees, early interstitial lung disease, scleroderma renal crisis with malignant hypertension).
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Anti-Centromere antibodies (highly specific for Limited SSc / CREST); Anti-Scl-70 / Anti-topoisomerase I (associated with Diffuse SSc & ILD); Anti-RNA Polymerase III (associated with Scleroderma Renal Crisis); Management: ACE inhibitors for renal crisis (life-saving!), Calcium channel blockers (Nifedipine) for Raynaud's, Cyclophosphamide/Mycophenolate for ILD.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Systemic autoimmune disorders causing chronic inflammation of skeletal muscle; Dermatomyositis includes cutaneous features and strong association with underlying malignancy.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Polymyositis: CD8+ T-cell mediated endomysial inflammation damaging muscle fibers. Dermatomyositis: Complement-mediated microangiopathy causing perimysial inflammation and cutaneous lesions.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Symmetrical, progressive proximal muscle weakness (difficulty rising from chair, climbing stairs, combing hair); Dermatomyositis rash: Heliotrope rash (violaceous periorbital edema), Gottron's papules (erythematous scaly papules over MCP/PIP joints), Shawl sign, Mechanic's hands; dysphagia; interstitial lung disease.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Markedly elevated Serum Creatine Kinase (CK) and Aldolase; Anti-Jo-1 (anti-synthetase syndrome: myositis + ILD + arthritis + mechanic's hands); Anti-Mi-2 (specific for DM); EMG showing myopathic triad; Muscle biopsy (gold standard); Management: High-dose oral Corticosteroids (Prednisolone) first-line, Methotrexate/Azathioprine as steroid-sparing agents.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Large-vessel systemic vasculitis predominantly affecting branches of external carotid artery in patients >50 years; strongly associated with Polymyalgia Rheumatica (PMR).
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Granulomatous inflammation of vessel wall with multinucleated giant cells causing lumen stenosis, ischemia, and risk of irreversible anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (blindness).
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Unilateral temporal headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication (pain when chewing), visual disturbances (amaurosis fugax, sudden painless vision loss), systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss). PMR: aching/stiffness in neck, shoulder, and pelvic girdles.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Markedly elevated ESR (>50-100 mm/hr) and CRP; Temporal artery biopsy showing granulomatous vasculitis with giant cells and disruption of internal elastic lamina; Management: Immediate high-dose oral Steroids (Prednisolone 40-60 mg daily; IV Methylprednisolone if visual loss) BEFORE awaiting biopsy results to prevent permanent blindness.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: ANCA-associated small-vessel necrotizing vasculitis classically involving upper respiratory tract, lower respiratory tract, and kidneys (triad).
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (c-ANCA / anti-PR3) activate neutrophils, leading to endothelial damage, necrotizing granulomatous inflammation, and small vessel destruction.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Upper airway: chronic sinusitis, nasal crusting, saddle-nose deformity, otitis media; Lower airway: hemoptysis, cough, dyspnea, cavitating pulmonary nodules; Renal: rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (crescents), hematuria, proteinuria.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: c-ANCA positive (Anti-Proteinase 3 / Anti-PR3 antibodies in >90%); Urinalysis showing dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts; Tissue biopsy showing necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis; Management: Remission induction with Cyclophosphamide or Rituximab + High-dose Corticosteroids.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Chronic systemic autoimmune disorder characterized by lymphocytic infiltration of exocrine glands (salivary and lacrimal); 9:1 female excess; primary or secondary (associated with RA, SLE).
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Lymphocytic infiltration (CD4+ T cells, B cells) and destruction of lacrimal and salivary exocrine epithelial cells leading to exocrine glandular dysfunction and dryness.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Sicca complex: Keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eyes, gritty sensation), Xerostomia (dry mouth, dental caries, difficulty swallowing dry food), parotid gland enlargement, extraglandular features (arthralgias, Raynaud's, interstitial lung disease, increased risk of Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma).
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Positive Anti-SSA / Anti-Ro and Anti-SSB / Anti-La antibodies; positive ANA and RF; Schirmer's test (<5 mm wetting in 5 mins); Ocular Rose Bengal staining; Minor salivary gland biopsy showing focal lymphocytic sialadenitis; Management: Artificial tears, artificial saliva, Pilocarpine (muscarinic agonist), Hydroxychloroquine for systemic symptoms.
